rationale: Phenotypic analysis from the primary cohort establishing Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas neurodevelopmental syndrome (OMIM #620985) demonstrates that hypotonia is present in 18 of 25 individuals (72.0%), directly falling within the hypothesized 60-75% range. Furthermore, behavioral and psychiatric anomalies, including autism spectrum features and neurodevelopmental impairments, are prominent core manifestations of pathogenic de novo MSL2 alterations.

evidence.text: In the defining cohort of 25 individuals harboring heterozygous de novo MSL2 variants, neurodevelopmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, and behavioral/psychiatric manifestations including autism spectrum disorder were key recurrent findings.

source.title: MSL2 variants lead to a neurodevelopmental syndrome with lack of coordination, epilepsy, specific dysmorphisms, and a distinct episignature
source.journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
source.quote: Using exome sequencing, here we identify a cohort of 25 individuals with heterozygous de novo variants in MSL complex member MSL2. MSL2 variants were associated with NDD phenotypes including global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, and motor issues such as coordination problems, feeding difficulties, and gait disturbance. Dysmorphisms and behavioral and/or psychiatric conditions, including autism spectrum disorder, and to a lesser extent, seizures, connective tissue disease signs, sleep disturbance, vision problems, and other organ anomalies, were observed in affected individuals.

evidence.text: Phenotype documentation for OMIM #620985 specifies that 18 out of 25 individuals presented with hypotonia, 21 had motor delay, 18 had speech delay, and 11 had coordination abnormalities.

source.quote: Twenty-one patients had motor delay, 18 had speech delay, 11 had coordination abnormalities, and 18 had hypotonia. Nine patients had seizures

evidence.text: Characterization of 3 individuals with protein-truncating MSL2 variants along with review of large-scale genomic studies supports the role of MSL2 disruption in syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders and autism spectrum disorder.

source.title: Novel protein-truncating variants of a chromatin-modifying gene MSL2 in syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders
source.quote: We reported first time the detailed clinical features associated with 3 MSL2 PTVs. There are 15 PTVs (13 de novo) reported from the large genomics studies (12 cases) or ClinVar (3 cases) of NDD, ASD, and developmental disorders (DD) but the specific clinical features for these cases are not described. Taken together, our descriptions of dysmorphic face and other features support the causal role of MSL2 in a likely syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder and add MSL2 to a growing list of epigenetic genes implicated in ASD.

evidence.text: Automated phenotype annotation lists hypotonia (HP:0001252) as very rare (1%), which directly conflicts with published clinical cohorts where hypotonia is present in 72% of patients.

conflicts: MalaCards lists hypotonia (HP:0001252) as 'Very rare (1%)', in direct contradiction to Karayol et al. (2024) and OMIM #620985, which report hypotonia in 18 of 25 individuals (72%). This discrepancy is attributable to automated ontology curation artifacts rather than verified clinical evidence.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact granular breakdown between truncal/axial hypotonia (HP:0008936) and generalized hypotonia (HP:0001252) across multi-center MSL2 cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: Existing publications frequently report general hypotonia (18/25, 72%) without specifically isolating whether axial/truncal weakness is predominant over appendicular hypotonia.

new_directions.question_text: How reliably can the distinct MSL2 peripheral blood DNA methylation episignature distinguish MSL2-related neurodevelopmental disorder from other MSL complex chromatinopathies (MOF/KAT8 and MSL3)?
new_directions.rationale: Clinical phenotypes (hypotonia, motor coordination defects, ASD) significantly overlap across epigenetic machinery disorders, making molecular biomarkers critical for differential diagnosis.
